questions.question: Do the AC-CROSS-1 and AC-CROSS-2 property/interleaving tests genuinely generate and iterate over the declared spaces (duplicate-redelivery counts, crash-timing points, sync-timing points for AC-CROSS-1; apply-site x arrival-order combinations for AC-CROSS-2), rather than hand-picking one or two representative sequences and calling it a 'property test' in name only? Would a test that only exercises the zero-duplicates/no-crash/already-synced happy path (trivially satisfied by any correct-looking implementation) pass under this suite, or does the generator space genuinely include the adversarial timing points the AC names?

Does this story verify against the REAL, already-implemented S5 (decline-b)/S6 (decline-a)/S8 (immutability-receive) production code — with no mocks, stubs, or fakes standing in for any of the three modules' actual logic — consistent with its exemption from the one-module-per-story rule (an integration story is licensed to reach across modules to verify the assembled whole, never to re-implement logic another module owns)? Confirm no new production logic was added anywhere by this story (per its scope exclusion), only test/harness code.

Could this integration story's verification surface be deleted and rewritten without modifying any file outside its `dependencies_allowed` list (the union of its owned ACs' `Spans modules:` set — decline-a, decline-b for AC-CROSS-1; immutability-receive for AC-CROSS-2, per acceptance-criteria.md and stories.json's `cross_cutting_acs`)? If not, which cross-module dependencies exist and do they flow through declared seam contracts (`DeclineGiftWrapPayload`, `InviteLifecycleContent`) in architecture.md, rather than reaching into internal implementation details of S5/S6/S8 that those stories' own contracts don't expose?

Are the AC-CROSS-1 and AC-CROSS-2 tests structured as genuine property/interleaving tests (e.g. parameterized over the cartesian product of the named dimensions, or using a property-testing framework's generator/shrinking machinery) rather than a fixed enumerated list of a handful of manually-chosen cases mislabeled as covering 'the space'? Does the test harness simulate crash/restart (process-level or state-reset simulation) and out-of-order `onHistorySynced` firing as REAL asynchronous interleavings, not just sequential function calls in a convenient order that never actually exercises the hazard?

Does this story's verification match the spec's/architecture.md's framing that it establishes the property-level guarantees which S10's e2e pass then merely conformance-confirms for one representative interleaving — i.e. is this the PRIMARY search over the ordering/interleaving space (not deferred to S10, which explicitly excludes the combinatorial search per its own scope), and does it produce a durable, re-runnable test artifact (not a one-off manual exploration that leaves no regression protection)?

Across the full AC-CROSS-1 interleaving space, is there NO interleaving that produces more than one `declined` post or more than one MLS Remove for the same invitee/group (double-removal or double-announcement would be an observable correctness/security regression, not just cosmetic), and across the full AC-CROSS-2 space, does the admin-carve-out gate hold uniformly — i.e. no apply-site x arrival-order combination exists where a non-admin-sourced delete/tombstone is honored, or where an edit-into-announcement (by target or by replacement content) slips through? Provide the specific assertion(s) that would fail if a single combination in either space violated the gate.

For any interleaving drawn from {zero-or-more duplicate redeliveries of a single decline gift wrap} x {zero-or-more crash/restart events, before or after DD-10 step 1} x {historical-sync completion before/during/after gift-wrap delivery}, does the system converge to AT MOST ONE `declined` post and AT MOST ONE MLS Remove per invitee/group, and to EXACTLY ONE of each whenever at least one delivered decline found the invitee still pending at some evaluation time? Provide (a) the generator/parameterization covering all three named dimensions against the real S5/S6 code, (b) the specific assertions checking both the 'at most one' bound (no interleaving ever produces two) and the 'exactly one when pending-at-some-point' floor (no interleaving ever produces zero when it shouldn't), and (c) confirmation crash/restart is simulated as a genuine interruption of the async flow (e.g. killing/reconstructing state mid-sequence), not merely omitted from the test.

For any apply site drawn from {direct `applyDeleteEditSignal`, buffered `resolvePendingSignalsForSlot`, TTL-expiry materialization, tombstone path} x any arrival order (signal-before-target, target-before-signal), does a delete/tombstone signal targeting a non-`image` `StructuredContent` message get honored if and only if the signal's sender is a current group admin at evaluation time, and is an edit signal whose target OR replacement content parses as non-`image` structured content always rejected regardless of apply site or arrival order? Provide (a) the generator/parameterization covering all four sites x both arrival orders against the real S8 code (8 combinations minimum for the delete/tombstone half, plus the edit-rejection half), (b) the specific admin/non-admin and edit-rejection assertions per combination, and (c) confirmation the buffered and TTL-expiry sites are genuinely exercised with signal-before-target ordering (the ordering these paths exist specifically to handle), not only signal-after-target which the direct path already covers trivially.

The story brief suggested vi.resetModules() + re-import as a technique to simulate an app restart resetting welcomeSubscription.ts's session-lifetime Maps (historySyncedGroupIds, declineProcessingChains). Implementation found this unnecessary: by inspection, applyDecline's only genuinely-throwing step is the MLS commit() call itself (modeled via commitBehavior: ['throw','succeed']); every step after a successful commit (sendAnnouncement, clearPendingDirectInvite) is internally try/caught and non-rethrowing, so a crash strictly between 'Remove commits' and 'mark-seen persists' cannot be injected as a distinguishable state via any black-box mock. Was the fallback (replay-after-restart via the tree-membership gate, i.e. deliver a second eventId against the same mutated members array without resetModules) actually load-bearing, or would a naive test (single delivery, no crash dimension at all) have passed equally well against a broken implementation? Verify the crash-before-commit scenario (commitBehavior: ['throw','succeed']) is the one doing real work: temporarily forcing commit to always succeed on first try should make the 'commitAttempts()===2' assertions in crossCuttingDeclineConvergence.test.ts fail, confirming they are load-bearing rather than vacuously true. EMPIRICALLY CONFIRMED during implementation: temporarily forcing commitBehavior to ['succeed'] only (removing the throw) on crossCuttingDeclineConvergence.test.ts made both the [crash-before-commit] and [concurrent double-click x crash-before-commit] tests fail (commitAttempts()===2 assertion), confirming the throw-then-succeed script is load-bearing, not vacuous. Change reverted immediately after the check; no production code was touched.

Implementation discovered that the TTL-expiry apply site's phase 2 (persistExpiredEntryEffect, chatPersistence.ts's sweepExpiredForThreadKeyLocked) structurally ONLY fires for targets with NO known row — it cannot evaluate a 'target-announcement' classification (the announcement-ness of a target that has not yet arrived) at expiry time, because there is nothing yet to classify. crossCuttingImmutabilityInvariance.test.ts therefore scopes its TTL-expiry it.each to the 'replacement-announcement' half of EDIT_TABLE only, with a comment explaining the target-announcement half's protection is enforced at the BUFFERED site instead (once the real target actually arrives). Is this structural-inapplicability judgment correct, or does it mask a genuine gap — e.g. could a target-announcement edit signal that ages past TTL with no known row, followed MUCH LATER by the real announcement target finally arriving, produce a materialized-then-overwritten row whose transient state (between TTL-materialization and the target's eventual arrival) is observable/exploitable in a way this file does not test? The buffered-site it.each (signal arrives, THEN target appends before TTL expiry) is not the identical interleaving as (signal ages past TTL with no known row, THEN target arrives) — confirm whether these two orderings are provably equivalent from the gate's point of view, or whether a fifth scenario is warranted.
